modules.title: Foundations & Preparation
modules.tagline: Most negotiations are won before anyone speaks.
objectives: Distinguish positions from interests and dig for the interests beneath a stated demand
Define and estimate your BATNA and reservation value, and use them to set a walk-away point
Map the ZOPA and identify when a deal is even possible
Build a written preparation sheet before entering any negotiation

lessons.title: Positions vs. Interests
glossary: position
What a party says they want — the surface demand ("I need $70k").
interest
The underlying need, fear, or motive that a position is meant to satisfy (security, recognition, growth).
issue
A specific topic to be decided in a negotiation, such as price, timing, or scope.

blocks.html: A position is what someone says they want. An interest is why they want it. This distinction, made famous by Roger Fisher and William Ury in Getting to Yes, is the single most useful idea in the field: positions clash, but interests often overlap or can be satisfied in more than one way.

Two people argue over the last orange. Split it 50/50 and both are half-satisfied. But ask why each wants it and you learn one needs the juice to drink and the other needs the peel to bake. Behind incompatible positions ("I want the orange") sat perfectly compatible interests.

head: Position
Possible interests behind it
rows: Fairness vs. peers, cost-of-living pressure, recognition, feeling stuck
A downstream client commitment, cash-flow timing, reputation risk
Margin targets, precedent for other buyers, internal cost floor

blocks.label: The magic question
blocks.html: When you hit a hard position, ask "What would that do for you?" or "Help me understand why that matters." You are trying to move one layer down, from the demand to the need.

Interests come in types: substantive (money, terms), process (feeling heard, having a fair procedure), and relationship (trust, ongoing partnership). Many stalled negotiations are really process or relationship problems wearing a substantive mask.

blocks.q: Someone insists on a Friday deadline. Which is the interest, not the position?
options: "We promised our own client delivery on Monday."
blocks.explain: The Monday client commitment is the underlying need. "It must be Friday" is the position — and once you know about the client, you might satisfy it a different way (a partial early delivery, for example).

lessons.title: BATNA, Reservation Value & Walk-Away
glossary: BATNA
Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement — what you will actually do if this deal falls through.
reservation value
The least favorable point at which you'd still accept a deal rather than walk to your BATNA; your walk-away number.
walk-away point
The concrete threshold that triggers you to leave the table and pursue your BATNA.
aspiration
Your ambitious but justifiable target — the outcome you're actually reaching for.

blocks.html: Your BATNA is what you'll do if there's no deal — the other job offer, the next-best supplier, keeping the house. It is the true source of your leverage: the better your alternative, the less you need any single deal, and the calmer and more credible you become.

blocks.title: How to build a BATNA
steps: List alternatives
Brainstorm every real option if this talk fails — even weak ones.
Develop the best one
Turn your strongest alternative into something concrete you could actually take.
Improve it
Can you make it better? A second job offer in hand raises your whole floor.
Estimate theirs
Guess the other side's BATNA too — whoever has the weaker alternative usually concedes more.

blocks.html: From your BATNA you derive a reservation value: the worst deal that still beats walking away. Cross it and you should decline. Above it, define an aspiration — an ambitious, justifiable target. Negotiators who set specific high aspirations consistently do better than those who just aim to "do okay."

blocks.label: Don't reveal your reservation value
blocks.html: Your walk-away is private. Reveal it and the other side will simply offer you exactly that. Reveal your BATNA only when it's strong and doing so strengthens your credibility.

blocks.q: An offer comes in below your reservation value. What should you do?
blocks.explain: The reservation value is defined as the point below which your BATNA is better than the deal. Accepting something worse means knowingly choosing the worse option.

lessons.title: ZOPA: When a Deal Is Possible
glossary: ZOPA
Zone of Possible Agreement — the overlap between the two parties' reservation values, where a deal can exist.
surplus
The total value created between the two reservation points, to be divided between the parties.

blocks.html: The ZOPA (Zone of Possible Agreement) is the range where both sides do better than their BATNA. A seller who won't go below $8,000 and a buyer who won't go above $10,000 share a ZOPA of $8,000–$10,000. Any price in there beats both walk-aways; the negotiation decides where in the zone the deal lands.

blocks.html: When reservation values don't overlap — the seller wants at least $11,000, the buyer will pay at most $10,000 — there is a negative ZOPA and no deal is possible at that moment. Recognizing this early saves everyone time; the move is to change the problem (add issues, improve a BATNA, expand the pie), not to keep haggling a single number.

blocks.q: A seller's floor is $9,500 and a buyer's ceiling is $9,000. What's true?
options: There is no ZOPA; no deal is possible on price alone
blocks.explain: The seller's minimum exceeds the buyer's maximum, so the reservation values don't overlap — a negative ZOPA. Any single price fails one side's walk-away. They'd need to add issues or improve an alternative.

lessons.title: The Preparation Sheet
glossary: preparation sheet
A written pre-negotiation worksheet capturing interests, alternatives, targets, and issues for both sides.

blocks.html: Preparation is the highest-return activity in negotiation. Amateurs improvise; professionals fill out a preparation sheet before every important conversation. It converts anxiety into a plan.

items: Interests — yours and (your best guess at) theirs, ranked.
Issues — every topic on the table, not just price.
BATNA — yours, improved as much as possible; and an estimate of theirs.
Reservation value — your walk-away number, kept private.
Aspiration — your ambitious, justifiable target.
Anchor — your opening, and the rationale that supports it.
Concessions — what you can trade, and what you want in return for each.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: "Getting to Yes" — Roger Fisher, William Ury & Bruce Patton
The foundational text on principled negotiation; introduces interests, options, and BATNA.
"3-D Negotiation" — David Lax & James Sebenius
Rigorous treatment of setup, structure, and BATNA-shaping away from the table.
Harvard Program on Negotiation (PON) — Daily Blog & Working Knowledge
Peer-informed articles and cases that keep the canon current with research.

blocks.q: What belongs on a preparation sheet but should stay private at the table?
blocks.explain: The reservation value (walk-away) is your leverage floor. Revealing it invites the other side to offer exactly that. Anchors are meant to be shared; the walk-away is not.

questions.q: Your leverage in a negotiation comes mainly from:
questions.explain: A strong alternative means you need this particular deal less, which makes you calmer, more credible, and able to hold firm.

questions.q: The difference between a position and an interest is:
options: A position is what you say you want; an interest is why you want it
questions.explain: Interests are the underlying motives behind stated positions, and there are usually several ways to satisfy an interest.

questions.q: The ZOPA is:
options: The overlap between the two sides' reservation values
questions.explain: The Zone of Possible Agreement is the range where both parties do better than their BATNA — where a deal can exist.

questions.q: A negative ZOPA means:
options: The parties' reservation values don't overlap, so no deal is possible on that issue
One side is negotiating in bad faith
questions.explain: When the seller's floor exceeds the buyer's ceiling, no single price beats both walk-aways. The fix is to change the problem, not repeat the haggle.

questions.q: What five-letter acronym names your best fallback option if no deal is reached?
questions.explain: BATNA = Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement — your fallback and the true source of your leverage.

questions.q: The four-letter acronym for the range where a deal can exist is ______.
questions.explain: ZOPA = Zone of Possible Agreement, the overlap of the two reservation values.

questions.q: Good preparation before a negotiation includes:
options: Deciding in advance to accept anything offered
Listing the other side's likely interests
questions.explain: Never pre-commit to accepting anything — that destroys your leverage. But knowing your BATNA, setting a walk-away, and estimating their interests are all core preparation.

questions.q: Setting a specific, ambitious aspiration tends to:
options: Improve outcomes compared with just aiming to 'do okay'
questions.explain: Research consistently shows negotiators who set specific high (but justifiable) targets achieve more than those with vague goals.

modules.title: Claiming Value: Distributive Bargaining
modules.tagline: When the pie is fixed, how you divide it is a skill.
objectives: Use anchoring deliberately and defend against extreme anchors
Plan a concession pattern that signals your floor is near
Justify numbers with objective standards rather than willpower
Recognize when to make the first offer and when to let them

lessons.title: The Power of the Anchor
glossary: anchor
The first specific number put forward, which biases the perceived range and pulls the outcome toward it.
anchoring bias
The cognitive tendency to rely too heavily on the first piece of numerical information encountered.

blocks.html: The first specific number — the anchor — exerts a gravitational pull on the final outcome. This is the anchoring bias: even people who know it's happening adjust from the anchor rather than ignoring it. A high but credible opening reshapes the other side's sense of what's reasonable.

blocks.label: Anchor with a reason
blocks.html: A bare number is easy to dismiss; a justified number sticks. Not "I want $110k" but "Based on the market rate for this role in this city and the P&L I'll own, $110k is the right level." The rationale is what makes the anchor hard to wave away.

blocks.title: Who should make the first offer?

cards.label: Anchor first when...
cards.html: You know the range well and can justify an ambitious number. First offers often set the reference point for the whole negotiation.

cards.label: Let them go first when...
cards.html: You're genuinely unsure of the range and the other side may have information you lack — their opening can reveal how they value the deal.

blocks.html: Precise anchors outperform round ones. An opening of $9,850 signals you've done specific homework and tends to pull the counteroffer closer than a round $10,000, which reads as arbitrary.

blocks.q: Why does a justified anchor work better than a bare number?
options: The rationale makes it harder to dismiss and reframes what's reasonable
blocks.explain: The supporting standard gives the anchor legitimacy. The other side has to argue with your reasoning, not just your number, which makes the anchor stickier.

lessons.title: Defending Against Extreme Anchors
glossary: re-anchor
To counter an extreme opening with your own justified number, resetting the reference point.

blocks.html: When the other side drops an outrageous anchor, the danger is that your brain quietly adjusts toward it. The defense is not to counter with a number right away — that would negotiate against their anchor — but to name it, set it aside, and re-anchor on your own terms.

blocks.title: Counter-anchoring in three moves
steps: Ignore, don't react
Don't reflexively counter. A quick counter treats their number as the real starting range.
Question the basis
"How did you arrive at that?" forces them to defend an indefensible number.
Re-anchor with a standard
Come back with your own justified figure: "Given comparable sales, the number that makes sense is X."

blocks.label: Beware the 'flinch' and the split
blocks.html: Two classic distributive traps: the flinch (visible shock designed to make you doubt your ask) and the premature "let's just split the difference" (which quietly makes the midpoint of two arbitrary numbers the deal). Splitting is only fair if both anchors were fair.

blocks.q: The other side opens absurdly low. Your best first move is to:
options: Accept it's the real range and adjust
Question how they arrived at it before offering your own justified figure
blocks.explain: Countering instantly anchors the negotiation around their number. Questioning the basis and then re-anchoring on a standard resets the reference point in your favor.

lessons.title: Concessions & Objective Standards
glossary: concession
Something you give up to move a deal forward.
objective standard
An external, independent benchmark (market rate, appraisal, precedent, cost-plus formula) used to justify terms.

blocks.html: Every concession should be deliberate, decreasing, and conditional. Decreasing: your concession sizes should shrink ($5k, then $2k, then $500), signaling you're approaching your limit. Conditional: never give ground for free — trade it. "I can move on price if you can move on the start date."

head: Concession pattern
Signal it sends
rows: "There's plenty more where that came from" — invites endless pushing
"I'm nearly at my floor" — realistic and credible
"My first number was inflated" — destroys anchor credibility

blocks.html: The most durable way to defend a number is an objective standard — market data, an independent appraisal, a published rate card, a cost-plus formula, legal precedent. Standards convert a contest of willpower ("I won't budge" vs. "neither will I") into a shared search for what's fair by an external measure, which both sides can accept without losing face.

blocks.label: Dialogue: trading, not caving
blocks.html:
Buyer: "Your price is too high."
Seller: "I hear you. The list is based on the independent appraisal. If timing is flexible and you can take delivery next quarter, I have room to move 4%. Does that work for you?"
The seller anchors on a standard, then trades the concession for something (timing) instead of giving it away.

blocks.q: Why should concessions shrink in size as you go?
options: To signal you are approaching your floor and can't give much more
blocks.explain: A shrinking pattern credibly communicates that you're near your limit. Equal or growing concessions invite the other side to keep pushing.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: "Never Split the Difference" — Chris Voss
Tactical treatment of anchoring, calibrated questions, and defending your number.
"Bargaining for Advantage" — G. Richard Shell
A research-grounded model of leverage, anchoring, and concession strategy.
"Thinking, Fast and Slow" — Daniel Kahneman
The cognitive science of anchoring and adjustment that underlies distributive tactics.

questions.q: Anchoring first is most helpful when:
options: You have no idea of the range
You know the range and can justify your number
questions.explain: A justified anchor set within a known range pulls the outcome your way. If you don't know the range, letting them open can reveal information.

questions.q: A concession should ideally be:
questions.explain: Conditional, traded concessions protect your position and train the other side that ground costs them something.

questions.q: The best defense against an extreme opening anchor is to:
options: Accept it as the real range
Question its basis, then re-anchor on an objective standard
questions.explain: Countering instantly negotiates against their anchor. Questioning the basis and re-anchoring on a standard resets the reference point.

questions.q: An objective standard is valuable because it:
options: Converts a willpower contest into a search for external fairness both sides can accept
questions.explain: External benchmarks let both sides concede to the standard rather than to each other, protecting face and legitimacy.

questions.q: A shrinking concession pattern ($5k, $2k, $500) signals:
options: You want to split the difference
questions.explain: Decreasing concessions credibly communicate that you are approaching your limit.

questions.q: The first specific number put forward, which pulls the outcome toward it, is called the ______.
questions.explain: The anchor exploits the anchoring bias — people adjust from the first number rather than ignoring it.

questions.q: Sound distributive (value-claiming) tactics include:
options: Splitting the difference of two arbitrary anchors
Using objective standards to defend terms
questions.explain: Splitting the difference is only fair when both anchors were fair; otherwise it rewards whoever anchored more extremely.

questions.q: The 'flinch' tactic is:
options: A visible show of shock designed to make you doubt your ask
questions.explain: The flinch is a reaction designed to pressure you into lowering your number without any substantive reason.

modules.title: Creating Value: Integrative Negotiation
modules.tagline: Before you divide the pie, make it bigger.
objectives: Distinguish distributive from integrative bargaining and know when to shift
Use logrolling and differences in valuation to create joint gains
Design and use contingent agreements and multiple equivalent offers
Balance the negotiator's dilemma of creating and claiming value

lessons.title: Distributive vs. Integrative
glossary: distributive bargaining
Win-lose negotiation over a fixed resource; one side's gain is the other's loss.
integrative bargaining
Negotiation that creates joint value by trading across issues valued differently.
fixed-pie bias
The mistaken assumption that the other side's interests are directly and fully opposed to yours.

blocks.html: Distributive bargaining divides a fixed pie: every dollar you gain, they lose. Integrative bargaining first grows the pie by finding trades across issues the two sides value differently. Most real negotiations are mixed-motive — they contain both.

blocks.label: The fixed-pie bias
blocks.html: Most people assume negotiation is purely distributive — that the other side wants exactly what they want. This fixed-pie bias is wrong more often than not, and it causes negotiators to leave joint value on the table. Assume there's a bigger pie until proven otherwise.

blocks.title: Two mindsets on the same deal

tabs.label: Fixed-pie thinking
tabs.html: "They want a lower price; I want a higher one. Whatever they get, I lose. This is a fight over one number."

tabs.label: Expand-the-pie thinking
tabs.html: "Price is one issue. What about volume, contract length, payment terms, exclusivity, delivery timing? Maybe I can give on the one that's cheap for me and dear to them."

blocks.q: The fixed-pie bias is the mistaken belief that:
options: The other side's interests are directly and fully opposed to yours
You should always make the first offer
blocks.explain: The fixed-pie bias assumes pure opposition and blinds negotiators to trades that could create joint value.

lessons.title: Logrolling & Trading on Differences
glossary: logrolling
Trading concessions across issues so each party gives on what it values less and gains on what it values more.
multi-issue offer
An offer that packages several issues together rather than settling them one at a time.

blocks.html: Logrolling is the engine of value creation: when two issues matter unequally to the two sides, each concedes on its low-priority issue to win on its high-priority one. The trick is to negotiate issues together as a package, not one at a time — settling issue by issue hides the trades.

head: Issue
Matters more to...
Trade
rows: Seller gives a little on price...
Seller prioritizes delivery, cheap for them off-season

items.label: Different priorities
items.html: Each side cares more about different issues — the classic logroll.

items.label: Different forecasts
items.html: You disagree about the future — resolve it with a contingent deal instead of arguing.

items.label: Different risk tolerance
items.html: The risk-averse party pays the risk-tolerant one to bear uncertainty.

items.label: Different time preferences
items.html: One wants money now, the other later — structure payments accordingly.

blocks.q: Logrolling creates value by:
options: Splitting every issue down the middle
Each side conceding on its low-priority issue to win on its high-priority one
Settling issues strictly one at a time
blocks.explain: Trading across differently-valued issues lets both sides gain more than a compromise on each issue separately. Packaging issues is what makes the trade visible.

lessons.title: Contingent Deals & Multiple Offers
glossary: contingent agreement
A deal whose terms depend on a future outcome ("if X happens, then Y"), used to bridge disagreements about the future.
MESO
Multiple Equivalent Simultaneous Offers — presenting several packages of equal value to you at once.

blocks.html: When two sides disagree about what will happen, don't argue — build a contingent agreement. "If sales exceed 10,000 units, the bonus applies; if not, it doesn't." Each side bets on its own forecast, and the disagreement itself becomes a source of a deal rather than an impasse.

Presenting MESOs — Multiple Equivalent Simultaneous Offers, several packages worth the same to you — is a powerful move. It signals flexibility, and the other side's reaction to the three packages reveals which issues they truly value, giving you a map for the final trade.

blocks.label: Dialogue: offering MESOs
blocks.html: "I want to find something that works for both of us, so let me put three options on the table. A: $95k salary, standard start date. B: $90k salary, a $10k signing bonus, and an early start. C: $92k, extra vacation, and a six-month review. Which direction feels closest?" Their answer tells you whether they value cash, timing, or flexibility.

blocks.q: A contingent agreement is most useful when the two sides:
options: Disagree about what will happen in the future
blocks.explain: Contingent ("if-then") terms let each side act on its own forecast, turning a disagreement about the future into the basis for a deal.

lessons.title: The Negotiator's Dilemma
glossary: negotiator's dilemma
The tension between creating value (which rewards openness) and claiming value (which rewards guardedness).

blocks.html: Here's the catch: creating value rewards openness (sharing interests so trades emerge), but claiming value rewards guardedness (concealing your reservation value). Push too hard to claim and you kill trust and the trades die; be too open and a hard bargainer exploits you. This is the negotiator's dilemma.

items: Share interests, guard limits. Be open about why issues matter; stay quiet about your walk-away number.
Reciprocate information gradually. Trade a small disclosure, see if they match it, then trade another.
Create first, claim second. Expand the pie together before turning to how it's divided.
Use standards to claim. Objective benchmarks let you claim value without appearing to grab it.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: "The Manager as Negotiator" — David Lax & James Sebenius
The definitive academic treatment of value creation, claiming, and the negotiator's dilemma.
"Negotiation Genius" — Deepak Malhotra & Max Bazerman
Research-grounded techniques for expanding the pie, contingent contracts, and MESOs.
"3-D Negotiation" — Lax & Sebenius
How to design deals and sequence issues to unlock joint gains.

blocks.q: The negotiator's dilemma is the tension between:
options: Creating value (rewards openness) and claiming value (rewards guardedness)
blocks.explain: Openness helps grow the pie but exposes you to a hard claimer; guardedness protects your share but can strangle the trades that create value. Skilled negotiators manage both.

questions.q: Integrative bargaining differs from distributive bargaining because it:
options: Creates joint value by trading across differently-valued issues
Is about winning at all costs
questions.explain: Integrative negotiation grows the pie through trades; distributive divides a fixed pie.

questions.q: The fixed-pie bias leads negotiators to:
options: Assume the other side's interests are fully opposed and miss joint gains
questions.explain: Assuming pure opposition blinds people to trades that could benefit both sides.

questions.q: Logrolling works best when the parties:
questions.explain: Different priorities let each side concede on what it values less to win on what it values more.

questions.q: A contingent agreement is designed to resolve disagreements about:
questions.explain: "If-then" terms let each party act on its own forecast, bridging a disagreement about future outcomes.

questions.q: Presenting MESOs (multiple equivalent offers) helps you:
options: Learn what the other side values by watching which package they lean toward
questions.explain: Equal-to-you packages reveal the other side's priorities through their reaction, informing the final trade.

questions.q: Trading concessions across issues valued differently by each side is called ______.
questions.explain: Logrolling is the core mechanism of integrative value creation.

questions.q: Ways to manage the negotiator's dilemma include:
options: Share interests while guarding your reservation value
Reveal your walk-away number early to build trust
Use objective standards to claim value
questions.explain: Revealing your walk-away early hands away your leverage; the other three balance openness with protection.

questions.q: Most real-world negotiations are best described as:
questions.explain: Real deals almost always combine value creation and value claiming, which is exactly what makes them hard.

modules.title: Principled Negotiation
modules.tagline: Be hard on the problem, soft on the people.
objectives: Apply Fisher & Ury's four principles of principled negotiation
Separate the people from the problem in emotionally charged talks
Invent options for mutual gain before deciding
Insist on objective criteria and use your BATNA as protection

lessons.title: The Four Principles
glossary: principled negotiation
Fisher & Ury's method: focus on interests and objective criteria rather than adversarial position-trading.
positional bargaining
Haggling over successive positions, which tends to be inefficient and to strain relationships.

blocks.html: Principled negotiation, from Getting to Yes, offers an alternative to positional bargaining (staking out and defending positions). It rests on four pillars, and this module takes each in turn.

blocks.title: The four principles
steps: Separate people from problem
Attack the issue, not the person; handle emotions and relationship separately.
Focus on interests, not positions
Dig beneath demands to the needs that can be satisfied in more than one way.
Invent options for mutual gain
Generate possibilities before committing — expand the pie.
Insist on objective criteria
Ground the outcome in fair external standards, not a contest of will.

blocks.q: Positional bargaining tends to be inferior because it:
options: Is inefficient and strains the relationship
blocks.explain: Trading positions locks people into demands, wastes time, and damages relationships. Principled negotiation targets interests and criteria instead.

lessons.title: Separate the People from the Problem
glossary: reframing
Restating a hostile or positional statement in terms of the underlying interest or problem to be solved.

blocks.html: People get entangled with problems. An attack on your proposal feels like an attack on you, and defensiveness follows. The first principle is to separate the two: address perceptions, emotions, and communication as their own track, so you can be hard on the problem while staying soft on the person.

blocks.label: Sit on the same side of the table
blocks.html: Literally and figuratively. Frame the talk as "us against the problem," not "me against you." "We both want this to work — how do we get there?" invites collaboration; "Your offer is insulting" invites war.

blocks.html: A key skill is reframing: when a positional or hostile statement lands, restate it as a shared problem. "You're ripping me off" becomes "So the price feels out of line with the value you're seeing — let's look at how it's built up."

blocks.q: "Separate the people from the problem" means:
options: Handle relationship/emotion as a separate track so you can be tough on the issue without attacking the person
Always concede to keep the peace
blocks.explain: The point is to protect the relationship while still pressing hard on the substance — not to suppress emotion or to cave.

lessons.title: Invent Options & Insist on Criteria
glossary: brainstorming
Generating options without immediate judgment, separating inventing from deciding.
objective criteria
Independent standards of fairness (market value, precedent, expert opinion, law) used to settle terms.

blocks.html: The third principle: invent options for mutual gain. The main obstacles are judging too soon, searching for a single answer, assuming a fixed pie, and thinking "their problem is theirs to solve." The fix is to separate brainstorming from deciding — generate widely first, evaluate later.

items: Invent first, decide later — no criticism during generation.
Broaden options — ask experts, vary the scope, mix in different issues.
Look for mutual gain — identify shared interests and dovetailing differences.
Make their decision easy — propose options they can say yes to without losing face.

blocks.html: The fourth principle: insist on objective criteria. When interests conflict directly, don't make it a battle of wills — agree to be bound by a fair, independent standard: market value, professional standards, precedent, cost, efficiency, what a court would decide. Frame it as a joint search: "What's a fair way to decide this?"

blocks.label: And if they won't play fair?
blocks.html: Principled negotiation is not naive. If the other side stays positional or uses dirty tactics, you have two protections: your BATNA (the power to walk) and negotiation jujitsu — don't push back on their position; ask questions, name the tactic, and redirect to interests and criteria.

blocks.q: The best way to generate options for mutual gain is to:
options: Evaluate each idea as it comes
Separate inventing from deciding — brainstorm widely first
Let the other side propose everything
blocks.explain: Premature judgment kills creativity. Separating inventing from deciding lets more and better options surface before evaluation.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: "Getting to Yes" — Fisher, Ury & Patton
The primary source for all four principles and negotiation jujitsu.
"Getting Past No" — William Ury
A companion focused on staying principled against difficult, positional counterparts.
Harvard Program on Negotiation — teaching materials
Case exercises that drill the four principles in realistic scenarios.

questions.q: The four principles of principled negotiation include all EXCEPT:
options: Separate the people from the problem
questions.explain: Principled negotiation explicitly rejects the win-at-any-cost posture in favor of interests, options, and fair standards.

questions.q: Positional bargaining is criticized mainly because it:
options: Always fails to reach a deal
questions.explain: Trading and defending positions wastes time and strains relationships compared with focusing on interests and criteria.

questions.q: "Separate the people from the problem" advises you to:
options: Address relationship and emotion on their own track while being firm on the substance
questions.explain: You can be hard on the problem and soft on the person at the same time by handling the human side separately.

questions.q: Objective criteria are used to:
options: Settle conflicting interests by a fair external standard rather than a battle of wills
questions.explain: Independent standards let both sides accept an outcome as fair without either simply out-willing the other.

questions.q: The best way to invent options for mutual gain is to:
options: Find the one correct answer fast
questions.explain: Separating generation from evaluation produces more and better options before judgment narrows them.

questions.q: Fisher & Ury's method that focuses on interests and objective criteria instead of trading positions is called ______ negotiation.
questions.explain: Principled negotiation is the framework from Getting to Yes.

questions.q: If the other side refuses to negotiate on the merits, your protections include:
options: Negotiation jujitsu — redirecting attacks to interests and criteria
questions.explain: Matching dirty tactics escalates and abandons the method. Your BATNA, jujitsu, and naming the tactic keep you principled and protected.

questions.q: 'Sitting on the same side of the table' is a metaphor for:
options: Framing the negotiation as us-against-the-problem rather than me-against-you
questions.explain: It reframes the negotiation as collaborative problem-solving rather than a personal contest.

modules.title: Tactics, Counter-Tactics & Psychology
modules.tagline: Know the moves — and the biases that make them work.
objectives: Recognize common hardball tactics and deploy effective counters
Identify the cognitive biases that distort negotiations
Use framing, reciprocity, and calibrated questions deliberately
Protect yourself from manipulation while staying principled

lessons.title: Hardball Tactics and Their Counters
glossary: good cop / bad cop
A tactic where one negotiator is hostile and another friendly, to make concessions to the 'good cop' feel like relief.
nibble
Asking for a small extra concession after the deal seems settled.
highball / lowball
An extreme opening offer intended to reset expectations.

blocks.html: Hardball tactics work by manufacturing pressure. The defense is almost always the same: slow down, name it, and redirect to the merits. A tactic loses most of its power the moment it's identified out loud.

tabs.label: Good cop / bad cop
tabs.html:
Tactic: one hostile, one friendly, so you concede to the 'nice' one out of relief.
Counter: name it ("Are you two doing good-cop/bad-cop?") and insist all decisions rest on objective criteria, not mood.

tabs.label: The nibble
tabs.html:
Tactic: after the deal's agreed, "...and you'll throw in delivery, right?"
Counter: "Happy to — what do I get in return?" Re-open the whole package rather than giving free add-ons.

tabs.label: Highball / lowball
tabs.html:
Tactic: an absurd opening to reset your expectations.
Counter: don't counter the number; question its basis and re-anchor on a standard.

tabs.label: Deadline / take-it-or-leave-it
tabs.html:
Tactic: artificial time pressure to force a rushed yes.
Counter: test whether it's real ("What happens if we need more time?") and fall back on your BATNA.

blocks.label: The nibble is expensive
blocks.html: Small end-of-deal asks feel too minor to fight over, so people give in — and skilled counterparts know it. Treat every nibble as re-opening the trade: a concession requested is a concession that must be bought.

blocks.q: The most reliable general defense against a hardball tactic is to:
options: Match it with a bigger tactic
Slow down, name the tactic, and redirect to objective criteria
Give a small concession to keep the peace
blocks.explain: Naming a tactic strips its power, and redirecting to the merits keeps you principled rather than dragged into a manipulation contest.

lessons.title: Cognitive Biases at the Table
glossary: framing effect
How the same option is judged differently depending on whether it's presented as a gain or a loss.
reciprocity
The social pull to return a favor or concession in kind.
overconfidence
Systematically overestimating your judgment, position, or the strength of your case.
winner's curse
The unease (or overpayment) that follows when the other side accepts your first offer too quickly.

blocks.html: Negotiation is applied psychology. Beyond the anchoring bias we met earlier, several predictable biases shape outcomes — in you and in them.

head: Bias
How it shows up
Use / defense
rows: People take fewer risks to protect a 'gain', more to avoid a 'loss'
Frame your offer as what they'd lose by refusing
A concession or favor pulls one back in return
Make a small concession to trigger one; beware manufactured 'favors'
Both sides overrate their case and their BATNA
Stress-test your own assumptions; ask for the other side's reasoning
A too-quick 'yes' means you left value on the table
Anchor ambitiously; never accept the first offer reflexively

blocks.html: The framing effect is especially powerful. Loss aversion means "You'll lose the early-renewal discount after Friday" motivates more than "You'll gain a discount if you sign by Friday" — even though they describe the same thing. Frame honestly, but frame deliberately.

blocks.q: If the other side accepts your first offer instantly, you've likely encountered the:
blocks.explain: A too-quick acceptance signals your offer was better for them than it needed to be — the winner's curse. Ambitious anchoring and not accepting first offers reflexively guard against it.

lessons.title: Calibrated Questions & Tactical Empathy
glossary: calibrated question
An open 'how' or 'what' question that invites the other side to solve your problem without triggering defensiveness.
tactical empathy
Deliberately understanding and labeling the other side's emotions and perspective to build influence.
labeling
Naming the other side's apparent emotion ("It seems like this timeline worries you") to defuse it and gather information.

blocks.html: Chris Voss's Never Split the Difference adds a tactical layer on top of the principled framework. Calibrated questions — open questions starting with "how" or "what" — hand the other side your problem to solve: "How am I supposed to do that?" invites help instead of triggering a fight.

blocks.label: Dialogue: a calibrated question
blocks.html:
Vendor: "Final price is $50,000, take it or leave it."
You: "I want to make this work. How can I possibly justify $50,000 to my team when the comparable quote came in at $42,000?"
You've made the vendor argue for you — and surfaced an objective standard (the comparable quote) at the same time.

Tactical empathy and labeling — "It sounds like the timeline is the real concern" — make the other side feel understood, which lowers defensiveness and surfaces information. This is not softness; it's a way to gather intelligence and steer the conversation.

blocks.q: What is the point of a calibrated question?
options: To trap the other side into a contradiction
To invite them to help solve your problem without triggering defensiveness
blocks.explain: Open 'how/what' questions engage the other side collaboratively and often lead them to argue your case for you.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: "Never Split the Difference" — Chris Voss
The source for calibrated questions, tactical empathy, labeling, and mirroring.
"Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion" — Robert Cialdini
The research behind reciprocity, framing, and other biases negotiators exploit.
"Thinking, Fast and Slow" — Daniel Kahneman
Foundational work on the cognitive biases discussed in this module.

questions.q: The most reliable defense against most hardball tactics is to:
options: Name the tactic and redirect to objective criteria
questions.explain: Naming a tactic removes its hidden power; redirecting to the merits keeps you principled.

questions.q: The 'nibble' is:
options: A small extra ask made after the deal seems settled
questions.explain: The nibble extracts free add-ons at the end; the counter is to re-open the trade and ask what you get in return.

questions.q: The winner's curse is the sense that:
options: Your offer was accepted too quickly, so you left value on the table
The other side has a better BATNA
questions.explain: A too-quick 'yes' means your offer was more generous than it needed to be.

questions.q: The framing effect means the same option is judged differently when presented as:
questions.explain: Loss aversion makes 'what you'll lose' more motivating than 'what you'll gain,' even for identical options.

questions.q: A calibrated question typically begins with:
questions.explain: 'How/what' questions are open and invite problem-solving; 'why' can sound accusatory and 'do you' invites a defensive yes/no.

questions.q: Deliberately understanding and labeling the other side's emotions to build influence is called tactical ______.
questions.explain: Tactical empathy lowers defensiveness and surfaces information.

questions.q: Good responses to an artificial 'take-it-or-leave-it' deadline include:
options: Testing whether the deadline is real
Falling back on your BATNA if it's genuine
questions.explain: Panic-signing is exactly what the tactic is designed to produce. Test the deadline, name the pressure, and rely on your alternative.

questions.q: Labeling (e.g., 'It seems like the timeline worries you') is used to:
options: Make them feel understood and surface information
questions.explain: Naming an apparent emotion defuses it and invites the other side to share more.

modules.title: Difficult Conversations & Emotions
modules.tagline: The hardest negotiations are the ones with people you can't walk away from.
objectives: Structure a high-stakes conversation using the three-conversations framework
Manage your own and the other party's emotions productively
Listen to understand and use acknowledgment before problem-solving
Preserve relationships while addressing hard substance

lessons.title: The Three Conversations
glossary: difficult conversation
Any exchange where the stakes are high, opinions differ, and emotions run strong.
contribution
Each party's part in creating a situation — distinct from blame, which is backward-looking and defensive.

blocks.html: From Difficult Conversations (Stone, Patton & Heen of the Harvard Negotiation Project): every hard conversation is really three conversations happening at once. Handle all three, or the talk goes sideways.

items.label: The 'What Happened?' conversation
items.html: The dispute over facts, meaning, and who's right. Shift from certainty to curiosity, and from blame to contribution.

items.label: The Feelings conversation
items.html: The emotions underneath. Unspoken feelings leak into tone and derail substance. Name them instead of burying them.

items.label: The Identity conversation
items.html: The internal stakes: "Am I competent? A good person?" Threats to identity trigger defensiveness — steady your own before the talk.

blocks.html: The single most useful shift is from blame to contribution. Blame asks "whose fault is this?" (backward-looking, defensive). Contribution asks "how did each of us contribute, and how do we change it?" (forward-looking, joint). Almost every conflict is co-created.

blocks.q: Shifting from 'blame' to 'contribution' means asking:
options: "How did each of us contribute, and how do we change it going forward?"
blocks.explain: Contribution is forward-looking and joint, which lowers defensiveness and opens problem-solving. Blame just triggers self-defense.

lessons.title: Managing Emotions
glossary: emotional flooding
A physiological stress response that shuts down clear thinking during conflict.
acknowledgment
Explicitly recognizing the other side's feelings or point before responding, distinct from agreeing with it.

blocks.html: Emotions aren't noise to be eliminated; they're data. But when someone experiences emotional flooding — heart racing, thinking narrowed — no rational deal is possible. The move is to lower the temperature first, then negotiate substance.

items: Name your own emotion to yourself — labeling reduces its grip.
Acknowledge theirs — "I can see this is frustrating" is not agreement, it's recognition.
Take a break if either side is flooded — propose a pause, not a walkout.
Slow the pace — silence and slow speech signal calm and buy thinking time.

blocks.label: Acknowledgment ≠ agreement
blocks.html: You can say "I understand why you'd see it that way" without conceding a thing. Acknowledgment makes people feel heard, which is often the precondition for them to hear you. Skipping it is why so many logically sound arguments fail.

blocks.q: When the other side is emotionally flooded, the priority is to:
options: Lower the temperature first, then return to substance
blocks.explain: A flooded person can't process a rational proposal. Calm first, negotiate second.

lessons.title: Listening and Reframing
glossary: active listening
Listening to understand, then reflecting back the content and feeling to confirm you got it.
mirroring
Repeating the last few words the other person said to prompt them to elaborate.

blocks.html: Active listening is the most underrated negotiation skill. Most people listen to reply; skilled negotiators listen to understand, then prove it by reflecting back what they heard before offering their own view.

blocks.label: Dialogue: listen, then reframe
blocks.html:
Colleague: "You always dump these projects on me at the last minute!"
You: "So it feels like the timing leaves you scrambling, and that's not fair. Have I got that right? Let's figure out how to give you more lead time going forward."
You acknowledged the feeling, confirmed understanding, and reframed a personal attack into a shared scheduling problem.

Mirroring — simply repeating the last few words someone said, as a question — keeps them talking and reveals more than any interrogation would. "...last minute?" invites them to explain, and explanation is information.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: "Difficult Conversations" — Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton & Sheila Heen
The Harvard Negotiation Project's guide to high-stakes personal conversations.
"Crucial Conversations" — Patterson, Grenny, McMillan & Switzler
Practical tools for dialogue when stakes are high and emotions strong.
"Nonviolent Communication" — Marshall Rosenberg
A framework for expressing needs and hearing others without blame.

blocks.q: The main purpose of reflecting back what you heard ('So it feels like...') is to:
options: Prove you understood, so the other person can relax and hear you
blocks.explain: Demonstrated understanding lowers defensiveness and is often the precondition for the other side to listen to you.

questions.q: The three conversations in every difficult conversation are:
questions.explain: Stone, Patton & Heen identify the substance ('what happened'), the emotions, and the identity stakes as the three simultaneous conversations.

questions.q: Shifting from blame to contribution is valuable because it:
options: Is forward-looking and joint, lowering defensiveness
questions.explain: Contribution asks how each side co-created the situation and how to change it, rather than assigning fault.

questions.q: Emotional flooding refers to:
options: A stress response that narrows thinking and blocks rational deal-making
questions.explain: When flooded, people can't process proposals — the temperature must come down first.

questions.q: Acknowledgment is:
options: Recognizing the other's feeling or view without necessarily agreeing
questions.explain: You can acknowledge how someone feels or sees things while conceding nothing substantive.

questions.q: Mirroring in a difficult conversation means:
options: Repeating the last few words as a question to prompt elaboration
questions.explain: Repeating the final words invites the other person to keep talking and reveal more.

questions.q: Listening to understand and reflecting back content and feeling is called ______ listening.
questions.explain: Active listening confirms understanding before you offer your own view.

questions.q: Good ways to handle strong emotions at the table include:
options: Naming your own emotion to yourself
Suppressing all emotion and pushing logic harder
Proposing a pause if someone is flooded
questions.explain: Suppressing emotion and pushing logic on a flooded person backfires. Naming, acknowledging, and pausing lower the temperature.

questions.q: The identity conversation is about:
options: The internal stakes ('Am I competent? A good person?') that trigger defensiveness
The legal identity of the parties
questions.explain: Threats to self-image drive much defensiveness; steadying your own identity stakes helps you stay grounded.

modules.title: Culture, Ethics & Trust
modules.tagline: Context, character, and credibility across the table and across borders.
objectives: Adjust your approach to cultural differences without stereotyping
Distinguish ethical persuasion from deception and coercion
Build and repair trust deliberately
Decide what to disclose, and recognize the cost of a damaged reputation

lessons.title: Cross-Cultural Negotiation
glossary: high-context culture
A culture where meaning is carried heavily by relationship, tone, and the unspoken.
low-context culture
A culture where meaning is carried explicitly in words and written terms.

blocks.html: Culture shapes what counts as a fair process, how directly people say no, how fast trust forms, and whether the deal or the relationship comes first. The goal is not a stereotype checklist but awareness of the dimensions along which cultures vary — then read the individual in front of you.

blocks.label: Don't confuse culture with the person
blocks.html: National generalizations describe tendencies, not individuals. A negotiator from a 'consensus' culture may be a fast unilateral decider. Use dimensions as hypotheses to test, not boxes to file people in.

A practical rule: in high-context settings, invest early in relationship and read the unspoken; in low-context settings, get specifics and terms on paper. When in doubt, ask about process: "How would you like to work through this?"

blocks.q: In a high-context culture, meaning is carried primarily by:
blocks.explain: High-context cultures rely on relationship and implicit cues; low-context cultures put meaning explicitly into words and documents.

lessons.title: Ethics: Persuasion vs. Deception
glossary: puffery
Vague, non-factual boosting ('this is a great deal') generally considered acceptable.
material misrepresentation
A false statement of fact about something that matters — generally unethical and often illegal.

blocks.html: You are never obligated to disclose everything, but you may not lie about material facts. The line runs between puffery ("this is a fantastic opportunity") and material misrepresentation ("we have three other offers" when you have none). The first is expected; the second is fraud.

cards.label: Generally acceptable
cards.html: Not volunteering your reservation value; puffery about enthusiasm; strategic silence; emphasizing favorable facts.

cards.label: Generally unethical
cards.html: Lying about material facts; inventing fake competing offers; misrepresenting your authority; false promises you won't keep.

blocks.html: Three lenses help when a tactic feels gray. The reciprocity test: would you be fine if it were done to you? The disclosure test: would you be comfortable if this appeared on the front page? The relationship test: what does this do to trust and your reputation over the long run?

blocks.q: Which is generally considered an ethical violation, not mere hard bargaining?
options: Declining to reveal your walk-away number
Claiming you have competing offers that don't exist
blocks.explain: Inventing fake competing offers is a material misrepresentation — a lie about a fact that matters. The others are accepted strategic behavior.

lessons.title: Building and Repairing Trust
glossary: trust
Willingness to be vulnerable to another based on positive expectations of their behavior.
reputation
The accumulated record of how you've treated past counterparts, which precedes you into future deals.

blocks.html: Trust is built in small, consistent increments and destroyed in a single betrayal. In repeated dealings — with colleagues, suppliers, family — your reputation is an asset that compounds. A reputation for fairness gets you better first offers and the benefit of the doubt; a reputation for sharp practice makes every future deal harder.

blocks.title: Building trust deliberately
steps: Make small commitments and keep them
Reliability on little things earns credibility on big ones.
Reciprocate disclosure
Share information gradually and match what the other side offers.
Be transparent about constraints
"Here's what I genuinely can't do, and why" builds more trust than bluffing.
Repair fast when you slip
Acknowledge, don't rationalize; a clean repair can strengthen a relationship.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: "The Culture Map" — Erin Meyer
A practical framework for reading and bridging cultural differences in business.
"Bargaining for Advantage" — G. Richard Shell
Strong chapters on negotiation ethics, bargaining styles, and reputation.
Harvard Program on Negotiation — ethics briefings
Cases and guidance on the line between persuasion and deception.

blocks.q: Why does reputation matter in negotiation?
options: It compounds across repeated dealings — fairness earns better offers, sharp practice makes future deals harder
It only matters in legal disputes
It replaces the need for a BATNA
blocks.explain: Reputation precedes you into future negotiations, shaping how much trust and benefit of the doubt you receive.

questions.q: In a low-context culture, meaning is carried mainly by:
questions.explain: Low-context cultures put meaning explicitly into words and documents; high-context cultures rely on relationship and implicit cues.

questions.q: The safest way to use cultural dimensions is to treat them as:
options: Hypotheses to test against the actual person
A reason not to negotiate abroad
questions.explain: Dimensions describe tendencies, not individuals; use them as hypotheses, not boxes.

questions.q: Which is an ethical violation rather than acceptable hard bargaining?
options: Fabricating competing offers that don't exist
questions.explain: Inventing fake offers is a material misrepresentation. The others are accepted strategic behavior.

questions.q: Puffery refers to:
options: Vague, non-factual boosting generally considered acceptable
questions.explain: Puffery ('this is a great deal') is non-factual enthusiasm and is generally acceptable, unlike misrepresenting facts.

questions.q: Trust is best described as built:
options: In small consistent increments and destroyed in a single betrayal
questions.explain: Reliability accumulates slowly; a single betrayal can undo it, which is why reputation is so valuable.

questions.q: A false statement of fact about something that matters is called a material ______.
questions.explain: Material misrepresentation is generally unethical and often legally actionable.

questions.q: Useful ethical tests for a gray-area tactic include:
options: The reciprocity test (would you accept it done to you?)
questions.explain: 'Nobody will know' is a rationalization, not an ethical test. The other three genuinely probe whether a tactic is defensible.

questions.q: A reputation for fairness tends to:
options: Earn better first offers and the benefit of the doubt
questions.explain: Reputation compounds: fairness invites trust and better terms in future negotiations.

modules.title: Salary & Raise Negotiation
modules.tagline: The highest-hourly-rate conversation of your career.
objectives: Research market value and build objective standards for a compensation ask
Negotiate the whole package, not just base salary
Time and frame a raise request effectively
Handle common employer tactics and objections with poise

lessons.title: The Offer Stage
glossary: total compensation
The full value of a package: base salary, bonus, equity, benefits, retirement match, PTO, and perks.
exploding offer
An offer with a short, artificial deadline designed to prevent you from comparing alternatives.

blocks.html: A salary negotiation is one of the highest-leverage conversations you'll ever have: a few minutes of discomfort can compound into hundreds of thousands over a career, because raises and future offers build on your current base. Yet most people accept the first number out of fear. Don't.

blocks.label: Never negotiate against yourself
blocks.html: When asked "What are your salary expectations?" early, deflect to research and defer the number: "I'd like to understand the full role first — what range is budgeted for this position?" Let them anchor if you can; if you must give a number, anchor with a researched, ambitious figure and a standard.

Negotiate total compensation, not just base. Base salary is one issue among many — signing bonus, equity, annual bonus target, start date, title, vacation, remote flexibility, professional-development budget, review timing. This is a logrolling opportunity: if base is capped, trade for the issues that are cheap for them and valuable to you.

blocks.q: When first asked 'What are your salary expectations?' early in the process, a strong move is to:
options: Give your absolute minimum to seem reasonable
Deflect to the role and ask for their budgeted range
Name a number far below market to be safe
blocks.explain: Deferring lets them anchor or gives you time to anchor on research. Naming a low number early caps you against yourself.

lessons.title: Asking for a Raise
glossary: value narrative
A concise, evidence-backed account of the impact you've delivered, used to justify a raise.

blocks.html: A raise request is a negotiation with an objective-criteria core: your value narrative. Come in with documented impact (results, scope growth, revenue or savings, praise) and market data for your role. You're not asking for a favor; you're proposing that your pay catch up to your demonstrated value and the market.

blocks.title: Preparing a raise ask
steps: Document impact
List concrete accomplishments, ideally quantified, since your last adjustment.
Benchmark the market
Gather salary data for your role, level, and region.
Choose timing
Align with review cycles, after a visible win, when budgets are set — not during a crisis.
Anchor with a specific number
Ask for a defined figure backed by impact and market, not 'a bit more.'
Plan the fallback
If 'no' on base, ask what would earn it and when, or trade for title, bonus, or development.

blocks.label: Dialogue: the raise ask
blocks.html: "Over the past year I led the migration that cut our cloud costs by $180k and took on the two junior engineers' onboarding. Market data for a senior role at this level is $135–145k, and I'm at $118k. I'd like to bring my base to $138k. <mark>How do we make that happen?</mark>" — impact, standard, specific anchor, calibrated question.

blocks.q: The core of a strong raise request is:
options: A documented value narrative plus market benchmarks
Comparing yourself to a coworker's salary
blocks.explain: Impact evidence and market data are objective criteria that justify the ask. Threats and coworker comparisons tend to backfire; vague asks get vague answers.

lessons.title: Employer Tactics & Objections
glossary: budget-constraint objection
"There's no budget" — sometimes real, sometimes a tactic to close the conversation early.

blocks.html: Employers have a familiar playbook. Recognizing each objection lets you respond calmly rather than deflating.

head: Employer says...
Likely meaning
Your response
rows: "I understand base may be capped — can we look at bonus, equity, or an earlier review?"
"I appreciate that. What would need to be true, and when could we revisit with a concrete number?"
"Take it or leave it — offer expires Friday."
"I'm excited about this. To decide well I need until [date] — is that workable?"
Return to your documented impact and external market data.

blocks.label: The exploding offer
blocks.html: An exploding offer with a 24-hour fuse is a pressure tactic that prevents you from comparing alternatives. Most 'firm' deadlines have give. Ask for reasonable time; a genuinely good employer will grant it, and one that won't has told you something useful.

blocks.q: "There's no budget right now" is best met with:
options: Immediate acceptance of the current number
A calibrated question about what would need to be true and when to revisit
blocks.explain: Treating it as a timing objection keeps the door open with a concrete future checkpoint rather than closing the conversation.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: "Negotiating Your Salary: How to Make $1000 a Minute" — Jack Chapman
A focused, practical guide to offer-stage and raise negotiations.
"Ask For It" — Linda Babcock & Sara Laschever
Research on the gender ask gap and concrete tactics for requesting more.
"Getting to Yes" — Fisher, Ury & Patton
Grounds the raise ask in interests and objective criteria.

questions.q: Total compensation includes:
options: Base plus bonus, equity, benefits, PTO, and other perks
questions.explain: Compensation is a package of many issues, which creates logrolling opportunities beyond base salary.

questions.q: When asked your salary expectations very early, a strong move is to:
options: Defer and ask for their budgeted range
questions.explain: Deferring avoids anchoring yourself low and lets you anchor later on research.

questions.q: The core of a strong raise request is:
options: A documented value narrative plus market benchmarks
questions.explain: Objective evidence of impact and market data justify the ask far better than threats or vague requests.

questions.q: An exploding offer is:
options: An offer with a short artificial deadline meant to stop you comparing alternatives
questions.explain: The short fuse is a pressure tactic; most 'firm' deadlines have room if you ask professionally.

questions.q: If base salary is capped, the best move is to:
options: Trade for other issues like bonus, equity, title, or an earlier review
questions.explain: Capped base is a logrolling opportunity — negotiate the rest of the package.

questions.q: The evidence-backed account of the impact you've delivered, used to justify a raise, is your value ______.
questions.explain: The value narrative is the objective-criteria core of a raise request.

questions.q: Good practices in a salary negotiation include:
options: Negotiating the whole package, not just base
Accepting the first number to seem agreeable
Anchoring with a specific, justified figure
questions.explain: Accepting the first number reflexively leaves substantial money on the table over a career.

questions.q: "That's the top of our range" is best treated as:
options: Possibly an anchor — pivot to bonus, equity, or an earlier review
questions.explain: Base caps are often real but leave other issues open; redirect to the rest of the package.

modules.title: Capstone: Prepare & Run a Real Negotiation
modules.tagline: Put the whole method to work on something that matters to you.
objectives: Synthesize preparation, value creation, and value claiming into a single plan
Map interests, compute BATNA/ZOPA, and design an anchor-and-concession strategy
Conduct a real negotiation and self-assess against a rubric
Debrief systematically to convert experience into skill

lessons.title: The Integrated Preparation Plan
glossary: preparation plan
A single document integrating interests, BATNA/ZOPA, anchor, concession plan, and standards for a specific upcoming negotiation.

blocks.html: This capstone asks you to choose a real negotiation in your life — a raise, a salary offer, a vendor contract, rent, a car, a shared decision at home — and take it from preparation through execution to debrief using everything in this course.

Start with the integrated preparation plan. It combines the preparation sheet from Module 1 with the value-creation and value-claiming tools from Modules 2–3, and the standards and tactics from Modules 4–5.

blocks.title: Build the plan
steps: Map interests
Yours and theirs, ranked, in all three types: substantive, process, relationship.
Compute BATNA & reservation value
Develop and improve your best alternative; set your private walk-away number.
Estimate the ZOPA
Guess their reservation value; sketch the overlap where a deal can live.
List issues for logrolling
Every issue on the table, and which side values each more.
Set anchor & aspiration
Your ambitious opening and the standard that justifies it.
Plan concessions
What you'll trade, in shrinking steps, and what you want in return for each.

blocks.q: Your reservation value in the plan should be:
options: Shared with the other side upfront
Set privately from your BATNA as your walk-away threshold
blocks.explain: The reservation value is your private walk-away, derived from your BATNA. Sharing it hands away leverage; leaving it undefined invites you to accept a bad deal.

lessons.title: Running the Conversation
glossary: agenda
A shared plan for which issues get discussed and in what order.

blocks.html: Execution has a rhythm. Open by building rapport and proposing a light agenda ("Could we start by making sure I understand what matters most to you?"). Explore interests before trading. Create value (logroll, offer MESOs) before claiming it. Anchor with a standard, concede in shrinking conditional steps, and keep the relationship warm while pressing on the problem.

items: Open: rapport, agenda, and a genuine question about their interests.
Explore: listen actively, label emotions, ask calibrated questions, find the differences to trade on.
Create: put multiple packages on the table; look for logrolls and contingent terms.
Claim: anchor on a standard, trade concessions, use objective criteria to divide the surplus.
Close: confirm terms explicitly, summarize in writing, protect the relationship for next time.

blocks.label: When it gets tense
blocks.html: Fall back on the fundamentals: name the tactic, take a break if flooded, return to interests and standards, and remember your BATNA is your safety net. You never have to accept a deal worse than walking away.

blocks.q: In what order should you generally create and claim value?
options: Create value (expand the pie) before claiming (dividing it)
blocks.explain: Expanding the pie first means there's more to divide and preserves the collaborative climate that makes trades possible; hard claiming first tends to kill value creation.

lessons.title: The Assignment & Debrief
glossary: debrief
A structured post-negotiation review of what happened, what worked, and what to change.

blocks.html: After you run your negotiation, debrief systematically. The goal isn't to judge whether you 'won' but to extract learning: where did preparation pay off, where were you surprised, which tactics landed, and what will you do differently next time?

blocks.title: Assignment: Prepare, run, and debrief a real negotiation
blocks.brief: Choose a real, upcoming negotiation. Complete an integrated preparation plan (interests for both sides, BATNA and reservation value, estimated ZOPA, issues for logrolling, anchor with a justifying standard, and a shrinking conditional concession plan). Conduct the negotiation. Then write a debrief assessing your performance against the checklist below. Submit the plan, a summary of what happened, and the debrief.
items: A strong result shows a clearly mapped set of interests for BOTH sides, in substantive, process, and relationship terms.
A strong result shows a developed, improved BATNA and a specific, private reservation value derived from it.
A strong result shows an estimated ZOPA with reasoning about the other side's likely walk-away.
A strong result shows at least one value-creating move attempted — a logroll, a contingent term, or MESOs.
A strong result shows an ambitious anchor justified by an objective standard, not a bare number.
A strong result shows concessions that were conditional and shrinking, each traded for something in return.
A strong result shows the relationship was protected — people separated from the problem, emotions handled.
A strong result shows an honest debrief: what worked, what surprised you, and a specific change for next time.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: "Getting to Yes" — Fisher, Ury & Patton
Return to the source to align your plan with the four principles.
"Negotiation Genius" — Malhotra & Bazerman
Worked cases and preparation frameworks ideal for capstone planning.
"Bargaining for Advantage" — G. Richard Shell
Includes a bargaining-style self-assessment to inform your debrief.

blocks.q: The main purpose of a structured debrief is to:
options: Convert experience into transferable skill by extracting specific lessons
Assign blame for a bad outcome
blocks.explain: Deliberate reflection is how experience becomes expertise; the win/loss verdict matters far less than the lessons you extract for next time.

questions.q: An integrated preparation plan should include all EXCEPT:
options: BATNA and a private reservation value
An anchor justified by a standard
questions.explain: You work from estimates of the other side, not private information you can't have. Interests, BATNA, reservation value, and a justified anchor are all core.

questions.q: In execution, you should generally create value:
questions.explain: Expanding the pie first leaves more to divide and preserves the collaborative climate.

questions.q: Your reservation value should be:
options: Kept private and derived from your BATNA
questions.explain: It's your private walk-away threshold, derived from your best alternative.

questions.q: A value-creating move in your negotiation could be:
options: A logroll, a contingent term, or offering MESOs
questions.explain: Logrolls, contingent agreements, and multiple equivalent offers all expand joint value.

questions.q: The purpose of the capstone debrief is to:
options: Extract specific, transferable lessons for next time
questions.explain: Structured reflection turns a single experience into durable skill.

questions.q: The structured post-negotiation review of what worked and what to change is called a ______.
questions.explain: The debrief converts experience into learning.

questions.q: A strong capstone performance demonstrates:
options: A specific reservation value derived from a developed BATNA
Revealing your walk-away to build rapport
Conditional, shrinking concessions traded for return value
questions.explain: Revealing your walk-away hands away leverage. The other three are hallmarks of skilled preparation and execution.

questions.q: Closing a negotiation well includes:
options: Leaving terms vague to stay flexible
Confirming terms explicitly and summarizing in writing
questions.explain: Explicit confirmation and a written summary prevent later disputes and protect the relationship.

questions.q: Real leverage in a negotiation comes mainly from:
questions.explain: Your best alternative is your leverage: the better it is, the less you need any single deal.

questions.q: Interests are:
questions.explain: Interests are the 'why' behind positions and can usually be satisfied in more than one way.

questions.q: The ZOPA is the range where:
options: The seller makes the most profit
Both parties do better than their BATNA
questions.explain: The Zone of Possible Agreement is the overlap of the two reservation values.

questions.q: A justified anchor works better than a bare number because:
options: The supporting rationale makes it harder to dismiss
questions.explain: A standard gives the anchor legitimacy the other side must argue against.

questions.q: The best defense against an extreme opening anchor is to:
options: Question its basis, then re-anchor on a standard
questions.explain: Countering instantly negotiates against their anchor; questioning and re-anchoring resets the reference point.

questions.q: Logrolling creates value by:
options: Splitting every issue down the middle
Trading across issues each side values differently
Settling one issue at a time
questions.explain: Each side concedes on its low-priority issue to gain on its high-priority one.

questions.q: The fixed-pie bias is the mistaken belief that:
options: The other side's interests are fully opposed to yours
questions.explain: Assuming pure opposition blinds negotiators to joint gains.

questions.q: A contingent agreement is most useful when the parties:
options: Disagree about what will happen in the future
questions.explain: 'If-then' terms let each side act on its own forecast.

questions.q: The four principles of principled negotiation include all EXCEPT:
questions.explain: Principled negotiation rejects win-at-any-cost in favor of interests, options, and fair standards.

questions.q: 'Separate the people from the problem' means:
options: Handle relationship and emotion separately so you can be firm on the substance
Never negotiate with people you like
questions.explain: Be hard on the problem and soft on the person at the same time.

questions.q: The winner's curse is the sense that:
options: Your offer was accepted too quickly, leaving value behind
questions.explain: A too-quick 'yes' means the offer was more generous than needed.

questions.q: A calibrated question typically starts with:
questions.explain: 'How/what' questions are open and invite the other side to solve your problem.

questions.q: The three conversations in a difficult conversation are:

questions.q: Shifting from blame to contribution is valuable because it:
options: Is forward-looking and joint, lowering defensiveness
questions.explain: Contribution asks how each side co-created the situation and how to change it.

questions.q: In a high-context culture, meaning is carried mainly by:
questions.explain: High-context cultures rely on relationship and implicit cues.

questions.q: Which is an ethical violation, not acceptable hard bargaining?
options: Fabricating competing offers that don't exist
questions.explain: Inventing fake offers is a material misrepresentation.

questions.q: In a salary negotiation, you should:
options: Accept the first number to seem agreeable
Negotiate the whole package, not just base
questions.explain: Compensation is a package; capped base is a logrolling opportunity.

questions.q: An exploding offer is:
options: An offer with a short artificial deadline meant to stop you comparing alternatives
questions.explain: The short fuse is a pressure tactic; most deadlines have give if you ask professionally.

questions.q: You should generally create value:
questions.explain: Expanding the pie first leaves more to divide and preserves the collaborative climate.

questions.q: A concession should be:
options: Conditional, shrinking, and traded for return value
questions.explain: Conditional shrinking concessions signal your floor and protect your position.

questions.q: Your best fallback if no deal is reached is your ______ (five-letter acronym).
questions.explain: BATNA = Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement — your fallback and leverage.

questions.q: Trading concessions across issues valued differently by each side is called ______.
questions.explain: Logrolling is the core mechanism of integrative value creation.

questions.q: Sound negotiation practices include:
options: Revealing your reservation value to build trust
Focusing on interests and objective criteria
questions.explain: Revealing your reservation value hands away leverage; the other three are core skills.

questions.q: Ways to create value in an integrative negotiation include:
questions.explain: Assuming a fixed pie destroys value creation; the other three expand joint gains.
